summary: Describes requirements for extending an IPv6 /64 prefix from a 3GPP mobile interface to a LAN link, and gives two implementation examples.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone gets one block of internet addresses from the mobile network. This explains how it can share that block with other devices, like a hotspot does.

questions: share ipv6 prefix from 3gpp to lan
how do mobile devices share ipv6 addresses
subtitle: How a mobile device can share its single IPv6 address block with connected laptops and phones.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices receive a single /64 IPv6 prefix from the cellular network, but need to share it with other devices (e.g., via USB tether or WiFi hotspot). Older 3GPP specifications only supported DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation from Release-10 onward, leaving earlier devices unable to delegate addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile device receives a /64 prefix from the cellular network, then advertises that same prefix to connected devices using Router Advertisement. Two implementation approaches are shown: one where the device only gets a global address on the LAN side, and one where the device uses the same anycast address on both links with different prefix lengths.
tldr.outcome: Connected devices can autoconfigure IPv6 addresses on the shared /64 without requiring DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation. This enables IPv6 connectivity for phones acting as hotspots and other scenarios before full DHCPv6 support was available.

today: RFC 7278 is an Informational RFC published in June 2014. It documents two practical approaches for sharing IPv6 prefixes on mobile devices before full DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation support was ubiquitous. While DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation is now the standard method, these techniques remain relevant for devices running older 3GPP implementations or for understanding how mobile hotspots and tethering evolved to support IPv6.

sections.title: The Challenge
sections.content: In 3GPP mobile networks (GSM, UMTS, LTE), a mobile device (called User Equipment or UE) receives a /64 IPv6 prefix assigned by the network via Router Advertisement. The RFC describes how to extend this single /64 prefix from the cellular interface to a LAN link (such as a WiFi hotspot or USB-connected laptop). The main challenge arose because DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, the standard way to delegate a prefix to another link, was only optional in earlier 3GPP releases and not widely deployed. This document describes two practical approaches to share the /64 without DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, along with requirements that both approaches must meet.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone connected to the mobile network gets a list of addresses it can use. The phone wants to let other devices use addresses from the same list. This is like a mail carrier giving one house multiple address numbers so the whole neighborhood can use them.

sections.title: Requirements for Prefix Extension
sections.content:
Four key requirements ensure that prefix extension works correctly:

  • R-1: The /64 prefix from the 3GPP network MUST be made available on the LAN link, so LAN devices can use Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) to configure addresses from the same prefix.
  • R-2: The UE MUST defend all its IPv6 addresses on the LAN link by responding to Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) probes, preventing address conflicts when devices try to autoconfigure the same address.
  • R-3: The LAN link configuration MUST be tightly coupled with the 3GPP link state, so if the mobile connection drops or the prefix changes, the LAN configuration immediately reflects that change.
  • R-4: The UE MUST decrement the TTL (Time To Live) field when routing packets between the 3GPP and LAN links, following standard router behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone must share its list with neighbors, prevent two neighbors from taking the same number, stay in sync with the mobile network, and count down the hop limit when relaying messages.

sections.title: Scenario 1: Global Address Only on LAN
sections.content:
In the first approach, the UE does not use a global address on the 3GPP interface; instead, it moves the received global address to the LAN link and keeps only a link-local address on the cellular side. The UE receives the /64 prefix from the 3GPP network via Router Advertisement, then announces that same /64 to the LAN using Router Advertisement. The UE assigns itself one global address from this /64 on the LAN link and defends it with DAD. The 3GPP interface only has a link-local address, which is sufficient for the point-to-point communication between the UE and the 3GPP gateway.

This approach allows the UE to act as both an IPv6 host (with a global address for its own traffic) and an IPv6 router (forwarding traffic between links). However, moving the address from the 3GPP interface to the LAN interface can disrupt long-lived connections that were specifically bound to the 3GPP interface address, since that address no longer exists there.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone takes the addresses it got from the mobile network and gives them to the LAN. The phone keeps a secret temporary number for itself on the mobile side, and uses one of the real numbers on the WiFi side.

sections.title: Scenario 2: Same Address on Both Links
sections.content:
In the second approach, the UE keeps the same global address on both links by using anycast addressing: the address is configured as a /128 on the 3GPP interface and as part of a /64 on the LAN link. Both links route packets destined to this address to the UE itself, so existing connections bound to that address remain uninterrupted when the UE starts routing to the LAN.

This approach maintains long-lived data connections because the UE's address does not change when router mode is activated. However, it can complicate applications that do not support the same address appearing on multiple interfaces, and handling privacy extensions (which generate temporary addresses) requires care to prevent duplicates. When privacy extensions are used, temporary addresses must be synchronized across both links so they expire simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone uses the same address number on both the mobile and WiFi sides. This way, if something was talking to the phone, it keeps working. But some programs get confused seeing the same address in two places.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content: When a UE transitions from a host to a router-and-host, basic IPv6 Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) security functions SHOULD be applied. The /64 prefix provided by the mobile network is shared with all LAN-attached devices, which has privacy implications: other devices on the LAN can observe the common prefix. However, mobile-provided /64 prefixes are typically short-lived because devices re-attach to the network when moving, changing location, or restarting. Some mobile networks reset the connection regularly (e.g., every 24 hours), issuing a new prefix. Conversely, dedicated mobile gateways may maintain the same prefix for extended periods. Privacy-concerned users should take measures to avoid keeping IPv6 prefixes long-lived when this is a concern.
sections.plainLanguage: When the phone becomes a router, the neighbors can all see that the address block came from the phone, which tells them information about the phone. But the phone usually gets a different address block after a while, so this is often not a big deal.
